No. The story uses a conventional form: a linear, chronological, close third-person account of a single ferry crossing, told in traditional realist prose. It has no non-linear timeline, multiple perspectives, unusual narrator, documentary or epistolary format, genre blending, or typographic experimentation.

The open, understated ending (Ilse silently pocketing the phone) and the subtle parallel between the crossing and her inner state are skillfully done. But these are standard techniques of literary short fiction rather than structural innovation.
